newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine ex-general regrets torture not legalized.
newsitem.headline: Argentine ex-general regrets torture not legalized.

text.p: A former top Argentine general during the 1976-1983 military dictatorship has said the junta should have legalised torture.
Carlos Suarez Mason said in an interview with Noticias magazine, which was published on Saturday, that he did not think the dictatorship tortured anyone.
"I repeat that I don't think that torture existed. Maybe we should have legalised it to cover a few excesses, like the Jews, who carry out several extreme beatings a day," he said.

The 72-year-old Suarez Mason, who escaped from Argentina after the return of democracy to avoid trial for human rights abuses but was later captured in the United States, defended his own behaviour during the dictatorship.
"I never sent anyone to be shot. We did eliminate a few. I think that is more or less clear," he told the weekly magazine.
Suarez Mason was convicted in 1988 of 43 murders and 24 kidnappings. Along with other generals he was pardoned by President Carlos Menem in 1990 and now lives with his wife in Buenos Aires.
Human rights groups said up to 30,000 people disappeared during the dictatorship's "dirty war" against leftist guerrillas, many ending their lives being dumped out of navy planes over the Atlantic.
